prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its active form, which made incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: My scientific case is unchanged after the full first-round exchange. B003 is a continuous arc from gut-hormone physiology (Holst on secretion and action of GLP-1 in humans, Drucker on proglucagon-derived peptide biology, receptor biology and the therapeutic concept, Mojsov on the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide) to large, durable benefit confirmed in independent outcome trials for diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal disease. The mechanism has been replicated for decades, so maturity is not in doubt. The central appetite-regulating actions also make it general physiology and not only a drug story. All six of us converged from the same evidence, which Linnarsson rightly says is not independent confirmation, so I rest the case on the experiments and not on the count. A single part with a three-person discovery core is the most coherent configuration on the shortlist. I do not see a second part that would strengthen it. Each candidate for one still needs something unresolved: Eshhar's credit for B015, the PERK and ATF6 arms for B043, the six-name problem for B036, and shorter follow-up for B040.
statement.case_against: Attribution is still the weak point and the round-1 exchange did not resolve it. Priority for identifying and synthesising the active peptide (Mojsov versus the Habener group, who are outside the credited names) is contested, and I cannot settle it from the supplied record. Leaving out Knudsen omits the person most responsible for liraglutide and semaglutide, so the configuration can be read as favouring discovery over the work that reached patients. Long-term safety of chronic use is still accruing. If the committee cannot defend Mojsov on the documented record, the trio is weaker than the unanimous round-1 agreement suggests, and the citation would need to be narrowed.

responses.point: The chair preferred Knudsen to Mojsov at opening, still calls the third seat open, and asks whether B003 honours discovery only or also drug development.
responses.response: I have reconsidered the Knudsen option seriously and still keep Mojsov. The shortlist entry does cover development, so Knudsen's claim is legitimate. But her contribution is the chemistry that made long-acting analogues from a peptide whose active form was already known, so it follows from the discovery layer. Without the identification of GLP-1(7-36) the rational basis for those drugs is missing. A contested priority claim calls for careful citation wording, not removal. That is why the citation names the physiology of GLP-1 and its active form and does not say who first identified the peptide. My answer to your question is discovery only. The committee should say so explicitly and record that development of the long-acting agonists is an application of that physiology and not a later prize part. I would change my position only if a majority wants a physiology-plus-development prize, and the three-person cap makes that awkward.

responses.point: Perlmann ranks B043 (Walter and Mori) second as the cleanest conceptual advance and asks whether a basic-science second part would strengthen or dilute a prize with strong consensus.
responses.response: I agree that B043 is the cleanest basic-science candidate and that Walter and Mori is the least contested pair on the list. I still would not add it as a second part this year. The chair's question is whether a second part needs demonstrated clinical consequence. I would not require that of a conceptual discovery in general. But in this case the human relevance is asserted more than demonstrated, and the PERK and ATF6 arms of the response (Ron, Harding, Kaufman) lie outside the credited names, so a Walter and Mori citation would honour only one arm of the pathway. Pairing it with a mature, outcome-proven discovery would not help either. I would take B043 seriously in a later year, and I would want the citation to cover the pathway and not just IRE1. Settling that is more important to me than the year it is awarded.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranks B010 (imatinib) third as mature and arguably overdue, and asks whether a second part with B015 is worth pursuing.
responses.response: I take the point that B010 is mature and that no one disputes the clinical benefit. My hesitation is the credit and the novelty of the concept. The upstream work on the Philadelphia chromosome and BCR-ABL (Rowley, Baltimore and others) is outside Druker, Sawyers and Lydon, and targeted therapy for CML sits close to what earlier prizes recognised. That makes it a strong translational achievement but a weaker discovery case than B003. On B015, I agree it is the most serious clinical candidate for a second part. But the citation cannot imply that the chimeric receptor concept originated with June, Sadelain and Rosenberg without crediting Eshhar, and I do not think the committee can resolve that from the supplied names. For that reason I keep B015 as an alternative and not as a second part.

responses.point: Linnarsson ranks B040 (Krainer and Bennett) third as a clean pair and ranks optogenetics sixth. He also notes that our convergence on B003 may reflect shared reasoning from the same evidence.
responses.response: I accept your caution about convergence and have tried to test B003 on its own terms and not on the count. On B040, the pair is clean and the clinical effect is unambiguous, but the approval dates only from 2016, durability is still being established, and the SMN1 gene discoverers are outside the credited names, so I treat it as a strong candidate for a later year. On optogenetics, I still regard it as a transformative method that changed how causal questions about circuits are asked, but I accept that a method weighs less than a disease-level advance. I also accept the chair's point that no trio of the six credited names is defensible without omitting someone with a decisive claim. I declare that this is close to my own field. I therefore keep B036 as an alternative only and do not argue for it ahead of B003.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's contribution to the active GLP-1 peptide can be credited without ignoring the Habener group, who are outside the supplied names. I could not check this independently.
Whether the committee will state explicitly that B003 honours discovery and not drug development, and what reason it would give for leaving out Knudsen.
For B036, whether a defensible trio exists among the six credited names, given the contested priority between channelrhodopsin discovery and neuronal deployment and Miesenböck's earlier approach.
Whether a second part would have been better supported if Eshhar's credit (B015) or the PERK and ATF6 arms (B043) could be resolved.
statement.conflict_note: I work in motor-circuit neuroscience, so the optogenetics candidate (B036) is in a field close to mine. I have applied the common criteria and do not rank it above B003. I co-authored a 2019 review with Sten Grillner and a 2009 paper with Thomas Perlmann. Neither is a candidate on any shortlisted ballot, and I do not regard these as recusal grounds. I have no new disclosure after round 1, and none of Drucker, Holst or Mojsov is linked to me through any documented connection.
